extracted.intended_audience: students, legislators, and readers of political philosophy interested in designing education and laws according to regime type
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and normative criteria for designing education systems and laws that fit the governing principle of different regimes (republic, monarchy, despotism), with concrete institutional recommendations and examples from ancient and modern practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws and education must be relative to the principle of each government
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws the legislator gives to society and the laws of education must be related to the fundamental principle of the government; matching them tends all the springs of government and gives the principle renewed force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This alignment is compared to physical action and reaction: when laws and education correspond to the regime's principle, they reinforce the government; subsequent chapters analyze this relation for each type of government (republic, monarchy, despotism).

rubrics_metrics.name: In monarchies, 'honour' mediates virtues and prescribes duties
rubrics_metrics.description: In monarchy the sentiment of honour pervades thinking and feeling and directs principles; honour makes virtues whatever it wishes and sets rules for what is prescribed to us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honour extends or limits duties as it pleases, whether those duties originate in religion, politics, or morality; education must conform to honour's supreme rules in a monarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honour limits obedience: princes must not command dishonourable acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Although obedience to the prince is fundamental in monarchy, honour dictates that the prince should never prescribe an action that dishonours the subject, since that would make the subject incapable of serving him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by historical examples (Crillon refusing to assassinate the duke of Guise; vicomte d'Orte refusing massacre orders): honour may permit refusal of certain commands and sets boundaries on acceptable obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nobility's duty to serve in war but with honour as arbiter
rubrics_metrics.description: Honour prescribes that nobility should serve the prince in war — it is their distinguished profession — but honour also claims the right to be its own arbiter; if honour is offended, it may permit or require retreat from service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honour allows nobles to accept or refuse offices and protects their liberty of choice above fortune; education of nobility must teach these honour-rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: In despotism education must produce servility
rubrics_metrics.description: In despotic states education seeks to abase the heart rather than elevate it; it must be servile so that those who command are tyrants who are also enslaved by custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good despotic ruler may prefer subjects to be servile even in command; education's goal is to produce obedience rather than civic virtue — begin by making a 'bad subject' to create a 'good slave.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme obedience presupposes ignorance in both ruled and ruler
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute obedience requires ignorance in the one who obeys and even in the one who commands: the ruler should not deliberate, doubt or reason; he should simply will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This frames the ideal character sought by despotic education: suppression of deliberation and independent judgment both below and above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despotism's education: instill fear and simple religious principles; avoid knowledge and emulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Education in despotic states is limited to living with others, putting fear into the heart and giving knowledge of a few very simple religious principles; learning and emulation are dangerous and emulation is harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that knowledge is dangerous in despotism, emulation is fatal to servility, and classical virtues (per Aristotle) are not fitting for slaves — thus education must be narrow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republican virtue is love of the laws and the fatherland; education must inspire self-renunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: In a republic virtue is simply the love of the republic — a sentiment that demands continual preference of public interest over private; education must be attentive to inspire this renunciation of self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This political virtue produces other private virtues; it is a feeling that can be possessed equally by the least and greatest citizen and must be formed by education and household example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental example is primary: fathers must transmit passions, not only knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: To inspire love of the republic in children the sure means is that fathers themselves possess and model it; parents are masters of giving their children their passions as much as their knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External impressions often undo household education; the corruption of 'men made' (the adult class) destroys the people — thus family practice is decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small states are required for communal/institutional systems like Lycurgus or Plato
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions such as communal property, banning money, and tightly controlled mores (those of Lycurgus, Minos, Plato) can only succeed in small states where a general education and close mutual oversight of citizens are possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large, complex societies cannot sustain the intense social regulation these systems require; the number, variety, and breadth of affairs defeat such measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban or limit money and luxury to restrain passions and preserve institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribing money and luxury reduces excesses that grow fortunes beyond natural bounds, multiplies desires and corrupts citizens; institutions that proscribe money aim to supply needs without multiplying desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Spartan-like institutions and recommendations (Plato's common goods, limits on commerce) which seek to give arts without luxury and needs without desires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cultural institutions (music, gymnastics) to shape moeurs and temper extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Music and physical exercises have political effects: musical modes can soften or inflame manners; gymnastics and martial exercises alone produce hardness and cruelty and must be tempered by music to cultivate gentleness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancients believed musical modes affect the soul; choice of musical education and gymnastic regimen should depend on the moral aim of the polity (e.g., tender music to temper martial rudenness).

rubrics_metrics.name: To establish equality in a democracy, laws must regulate inheritance, dowries, donations, and testaments
rubrics_metrics.description: An equal partition of land (as among Lycurgus or Romulus) must be supported by laws that regulate marriage portions, donations, successions and testaments; without such laws an initial equal distribution will be undone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: law forbidding multiple inheritances, rules that the nearest relative marry the heiress, limits on bequests — Solon's allowance of testamentary freedom contradicts equality aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit multiple inheritances and limit accumulation to maintain equal fortunes
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws that forbid having two heritages or limit the capacity to concentrate portions of land prevent re-accumulation of property and help preserve the original equality founding a republic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato and ancient practices required measures such as selecting one child as heir and giving others in adoption to keep the number of citizen land portions stable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate marriage and dowry rules to prevent concentration of property
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage customs (e.g., restrictions on marriages with uterine vs. consanguine sisters) and rules on dowries were designed to prevent land portions from passing into a single family and to preserve equal distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different city-states used different rules (Athens vs Sparta) with pragmatic adjustments (e.g., giving the sister half the brother's portion) to avoid improper concentration of property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a census and class categorization to fix and limit inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a cens/assessment (as Solon did) to reduce or fix differences at a certain point; after that use specific laws to equalize by imposing burdens on the rich and reliefs to the poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cens classes limit who may hold office and distribute responsibilities; extreme fortunes resist compensatory measures, so the cens must cap inequalities that allow compensations to work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow functional exceptions to equality when necessary for the republic's utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Some inequalities (e.g., for those who must work continuously and cannot afford magistracies, for artisans, or for numerous freedmen) may be permitted if removing equality in those cases serves the republic's utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such exceptions are 'apparent' removals of equality intended to preserve the overall functioning and stability of the democratic principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frugality must be institutionalized: keep land portions small and favor commercial spirit where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Frugality and equality reinforce each other: small land portions sustain frugality; in commercial republics, the spirit of commerce (economy, moderation) can permit wealth without corruption if laws and leading citizens favor that spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In commercial republics, equal inheritance shares for children promote frugality across generations; the legislator must create laws that divide fortunes as commerce grows to maintain citizens' need to work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a senate of elders as a fixed moral model to sustain republican moeurs
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a fixed body (a senate) whose age, virtue, gravity and services make it a rule of moeurs — senators should be seen as simulacra of the gods to inspire proper sentiments across families and magistrates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The senate should cling to ancient institutions and be preferably constituted for life (as in Rome, Sparta, or Athens' Areopagus) to provide continuity of moral example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme institutional remedies (Lycurgue/Plato-style) must be subtle so as not to alienate citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: Radical measures (e.g., forced redistribution, required gifts) to equalize fortunes may provoke hatred if made too explicit or extreme; sometimes laws should reach the goal indirectly to be politically effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phaleas' proposal (rich give dowries to poor, poor receive money but do not give) is cited as impractical because it imposes asymmetric burdens that citizens would resent; legislator should temper measures with prudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ancient institutions and custom are valuable corrective resources for moeurs
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserving and recalling ancient customs and institutions often restores virtue; old institutions are corrective and new ones often embody abuses — long governments decline by slow slope and recovery demands effort and return to old maxims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinforcing customs through a conservative senate and public example helps maintain moeurs; revolutions that established new forms typically required great laws to succeed and thus ancient usages are stabilizing.
